dispatch.headline: Oiled Levers Wrote Laws
dispatch.body:
Voters inside Olaru Terminal spent thirty years choosing station presidents based entirely on lever resistance.

A five-year health study found that heavy velvet drapes inside vintage polling booths trap stagnant air, causing microgravity oxygen levels to drop within forty seconds. By the time a citizen reads the ballot, mild hypoxia sets in, leading eighty-four percent of voters to pull whichever mechanical lever moves with the least effort.

Dr Morwenna Voss led the study.

"Voters are not rejecting quiet rooms or choosing policy," Dr Voss said. "They are trying not to pass out beside a curtain."

Maintenance logs reveal the reform party lever was greased during a refit in 2164, while the opposition lever remained unoiled. Every major policy since, including the end of weekend spin-gravity, was decided by a single tub of industrial lubricant.

The civic board refused to replace the velvet drapes before next month's public vote on selling the station water recycling grid, citing civic tradition. Selling the grid requires pulling lever two, which was freshly greased yesterday by the prospective buyer.
dispatch.scene: A voter in a padded grey jumpsuit leans weak-kneed inside a heavy velvet polling booth, reaching for a greased steel lever while drapes press tight around him.

glossary.gloss: Artificial gravity generated by rotating station segments on scheduled schedules.

dispatch.premise: A study of the High-Orbit Terminal's elections reveals that voters inside 1950s heavy-velvet booths routinely suffer mild microgravity hypoxia, leading 84 percent of citizens to vote for whichever candidate's mechanical lever requires the least oxygen to pull.

drafts.headline: Senate Passes Laws By Shaking Clock
drafts.body:
Dr Tariq Basu published his study of the senate clock after three senators collapsed from shoulder strain. His report confirms that station policy is decided by whichever party hires the strongest endurance athletes. Under chamber rules, a filibuster ends only when the 18th-century pendulum clock strikes three. Because the chamber sits in zero gravity, the pendulum stays motionless unless someone manually shakes the entire cabinet back and forth.

"The clock is legal," Dr Basu said. "It needs thirty shakes a minute."

Major parties now recruit exclusively from deep-space rowing teams. Debates on air rations last until one side suffers muscle failure. Last month, the reform bloc passed a waste pipe bill after hiring two triathletes to shake the wooden cabinet through the night. The minority leader attempted to object. His wrist gave out.

Dr Basu warned that the political process is shifting toward raw physical power. Both major parties have begun feeding their speakers high-calorie paste during floor speeches. Without a rule change, the habitat's next air budget will be decided by whichever side can maintain eighty shakes a minute through a torn muscle.
drafts.premise: Orbital sociologists studying the station's senate confirm that parliamentary filibusters are timed by an 18th-century grandfather clock that must be manually shaken in microgravity, leaving all station policy in the hands of whichever faction hires the strongest endurance athletes.

drafts.headline: Sun Votes To Keep Old Computers
drafts.body:
Dr Naomi Okafor holds a paper voting card up to the solar viewport. Her team at the High-Orbit Spire checked four hundred iron tally boxes built in 1964 that still count every station election. Heavy solar flares regularly punch fresh holes through the paper ballots during radiation storms. Radiation damage consistently strikes the card slot for candidates who promise never to buy new computers.

"It is simple heat," Okafor said. "The old brass arms expand when hit by solar flares. The pin slips three millimetres left and punches the box for keeping the old gear."

A major solar storm has hit during every election since 2110. Every winning candidate has cut hull shielding budgets to preserve station heritage. Station air smells of burnt wire. Last month's flare added six thousand votes for incumbent governor Peter Lindqvist, who ran on a platform of burning all computer plans.

"The machine works fine," Lindqvist said.

Engineers report that hull shielding will drop another four percent before the autumn primary. Cosmic radiation is projected to select the next chief engineer by nightfall.
drafts.premise: Data scientists at the High-Orbit Spire confirm that 1960s punch-card voting machines alter tally holes when hit by solar flares, though researchers note the radiation errors consistently favor candidates who promise to never upgrade the computers.

drafts.headline: Voting Wax Threatens Station Air Supply
drafts.body:
Engineers at Solis Anchor extracted eighty kilograms of dark wax from the central air intake on Monday. Senior ventilation analyst Dr Priya Nair warns that two centuries of sealing referendum ballots in hot beeswax under microgravity have reduced filter capacity to twelve percent.

Civic law requires every resident to seal their paper ballot with melted comb wax to ensure election security. In zero gravity, fine wax mist escapes the polling booths, drifts into the intake shafts, and hardens across the primary air scrubbers.

The station faces a complete loss of breathable air within six weeks. A public referendum on purchasing replacement scrubbers is scheduled for next month.

"The extraction fans will seize three hours into polling," Nair said. "The air will run out long before officials finish counting."

Station directors confirmed that cancelling the scheduled vote requires an official referendum. Under section four, that vote must also be conducted using hot wax seals.

"The rule is clear," Nair said.

"Citizens must choose."

She recommended taking a deep breath before entering the booth.
drafts.premise: Structural engineers analyzing the Lagrange Elevator Station warn that a 200-year-old requirement to seal referendum votes in hot beeswax in microgravity has steadily clogged the central air scrubbers, threatening total asphyxiation if citizens hold another public vote.

drafts.headline: Voters Picked Leaders By Lever Weight
drafts.body:
Voters inside the terminal chose four station presidents based on lever resistance.

A five-year health audit at Olaru Terminal found that heavy velvet drapes inside vintage polling booths trap stagnant air, causing microgravity oxygen drops within forty seconds. By the time a citizen reads the ballot, mild hypoxia sets in, leading eighty-four percent of voters to pull whichever mechanical lever moves most easily.

Dr. Morwenna Voss led the study.

"Voters are not choosing platforms," Dr. Voss said. "They are saving breath."

The findings mean thirty years of station law, including the end of weekend spin-gravity and the fee on quiet rooms, were decided entirely by grease levels inside the box. Maintenance logs reveal the reform party lever was greased during a routine refit in 2164, while the opposition lever remained unoiled.

The civic board declined to replace the velvet drapes before next month's public vote on selling the station water recycling grid. Board members noted that civic tradition requires keeping the booths unchanged. That proposal requires pulling lever four. Lever four rusted shut twelve years ago.
drafts.premise: A study of the High-Orbit Terminal's elections reveals that voters inside 1950s heavy-velvet booths routinely suffer mild microgravity hypoxia, leading 84 percent of citizens to vote for whichever candidate's mechanical lever requires the least oxygen to pull.

quality.judge_reason: Draft 2 lands a sharp satire on voter fatigue and rigged voting systems, anchored by a brilliant final kicker.
quality.critique: The original headline was purely descriptive rather than landing a joke, and the final line restated the mechanics instead of delivering a punchline. The revision sharpens the dialogue, tightens the comedic pacing, and ends on an active kicker.
quality.revise_judge_reason: The final line about the prospective buyer greasing the lever turns a quirky premise into a sharp satire on corporate bribery.
